extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers, theologians, philosophers, and scientists interested in the relation between religion and science
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance for how religion and science should relate and how thinkers should judge, reform, and tolerate religious beliefs while respecting epistemic limits. Addresses duties of humility, the social function of creeds, and principles for cultivating toleration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid trespassing on the other's province
rubrics_metrics.description: Religion should not claim positive knowledge beyond its remit, and Science should not include within the boundaries of knowledge that which cannot be known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text describes how Religion, by professing definite knowledge about mysteries, 'trespassed upon the province of Science', while Science, by substituting metaphysical entities and classing some incomprehensibles among the things it comprehends, 'trespassed on the province of Religion.' The implication: each domain ought to respect the limits of the other and refrain from asserting what properly belongs to the other's sphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual epistemic humility as condition for reconciliation
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'permanent peace' between Religion and Science requires Science to be 'fully convinced that its explanations are proximate and relative' and Religion to be 'fully convinced that the mystery it contemplates is ultimate and absolute.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sets the evaluative standard for both sides: Science should acknowledge the provisional, approximate status of its explanations; Religion should acknowledge the ultimate unknowability of certain matters. Reconciliation is measured by the extent to which each side accepts these limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refrain from asserting attributes of the Absolute
rubrics_metrics.description: Our duty is 'neither to affirm nor deny personality' of the Ultimate Cause; we must submit to the 'established limits of our intelligence' rather than perversely assign definite attributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text rejects the requirement to represent the Absolute under the familiar forms of our consciousness (e.g., Mansel's claim that 'it is our duty... to think of God as personal'). Anti-pattern: insisting on definite attributes for the Unconditioned despite evidentiary and conceptual limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat theological notions as symbolic, not literal
rubrics_metrics.description: We 'shall not err' in forming conceptions of the Ultimate Existence provided we 'treat every notion we thus frame as merely a symbol, utterly without resemblance to that for which it stands.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice for how to use religious language: construct symbolic ideas to give shape to vague sense of the Ultimate, but continually reject them as inadequate to avoid idolatry of concepts. The author endorses 'constant formation of such symbols and constant rejection of them' as a discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize a fundamental verity present in all religions
rubrics_metrics.description: In every form of religion 'there is a soul of truth' — a fundamental verity that gives vitality even to degraded creeds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When criticizing religious forms, remember that they often embody an underlying truth. This fact should temper condemnation and informs the practice of toleration: condemn forms but acknowledge the surviving verity within them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value concrete religious elements as relatively good
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete elements of religion, while imperfect by an absolute standard, are 'good as measured by a relative one' because they render abstract verities thinkable and influential to lower perceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text calls such elements 'protective envelopes' without which the contained truth would die. Anti-pattern: removing concrete motifs or rites prematurely, thereby leaving people with no effective motives or guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: See beliefs as necessary parts of the constituted social order
rubrics_metrics.description: Various religious beliefs are 'parts of the constituted order of things; and not accidental but necessary parts' — they are perennial and redevelop when cut down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion counsels taking the social and adaptive role of beliefs seriously. It supports wide toleration and the recognition that beliefs perform functions in societies and cannot be summarily dismissed as merely accidental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid premature substitution of abstract beliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: Refusal to abandon a relatively concrete notion for a relatively abstract one often 'implies the inability to frame the relatively abstract one' and 'so proves that the change would be premature and injurious.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: do not force abstract conceptions on populations until their experiences and education make such conceptions mentally realizable; new creeds 'become adequately operative only when... an element in early education, and has the support of a strong social sanction.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure beliefs are vividly realized to influence conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: The effects of a belief on conduct 'must be diminished in proportion as the vividness with which it is realized becomes less'; many require 'vividly depicted future torments and future joys' to be morally effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative standard for the practical efficacy of beliefs: the more concrete and imaginable the motives a creed supplies, the more influence it has on behavior. Reformers should account for this when judging or changing doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the social function of conservatism
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'adhesion to old institutions and beliefs' serves as a 'constant check' preventing change from being too rapid; theological conservatism 'has an all-important function.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This frames conservatism as a legitimate balancing criterion: evaluation of reforms must weigh risks of too-rapid change and the stabilizing benefits of existing institutions and beliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foster the widest possible toleration and do justice to alien beliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: Our toleration 'should be the widest possible' and should aim not merely to 'refrain from injustice of word or deed' but to 'do justice by an open recognition of positive worth' and to 'qualify our disagreement with as much as may be of sympathy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Behavioral rubric for thinkers: restrain indignation, listen calmly, avoid contemptuous condemnation, and actively acknowledge positives in beliefs one rejects. The author lists psychological difficulties but insists on tempering reactions in calmer judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the perpetual construction and rejection of symbols as discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Perpetually to construct ideas that strain our faculties and to find them futile may 'realize to us... the greatness of that which we vainly strive to grasp' and 'maintain in our minds a due sense of the incommensurable difference between the Conditioned and the Unconditioned.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prescribes an intellectual practice: symbolic thinking followed by critical rejection cultivates humility and reverence. It is an evaluative standard for how to engage with metaphysical speculation without mistaking symbols for realities.
